name: Dysautonomia ในลำไส้
preview_text: IBS isn’t one condition in TCM - it’s a family of six distinct patterns, each with its own cause and its own treatment. Most patients see significant improvement within 4-8 weeks o...
categories: ["ปัญหาลำไส้และลำไส้"]
synonyms: ["autonomic nervous system disorders affecting the intestines"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a chronic functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits - diarrhea, constipation, or both - without any visible damage to the digestive tract. It’s diagnosed using symptom-based criteria (the Rome IV criteria) after ruling out other conditions like inflammatory bowel disease or celiac disease.
IBS affects roughly 10-15% of the population worldwide, and while the exact cause remains unclear, factors such as altered gut motility, visceral hypersensitivity, gut-brain axis dysfunction, and changes in the gut microbiome are thought to play a role. Conventional treatment focuses on managing symptoms rather than addressing a root cause.
conventional_treatments: Standard Western management includes dietary modifications (low-FODMAP diet, increased fiber), stress reduction, and medications targeted at predominant symptoms: antispasmodics for pain, loperamide for diarrhea, laxatives or lubiprostone for constipation, and low-dose antidepressants to modulate gut-brain signaling. Psychological therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy are sometimes recommended.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, IBS is understood as a disruption in the harmonious movement of Qi through the digestive system, primarily involving the Liver, Spleen, and Large Intestine. The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, and when emotional stress, frustration, or anxiety cause the Liver Qi to stagnate, it can overact on the Spleen - the organ that transforms food into energy and fluids. This is the classic “Liver invading the Spleen” pattern, where cramping and urgent diarrhea strike after a tense meeting or argument.
But the Spleen can also be weak on its own, unable to manage fluids, leading to a buildup of internal Dampness. That Dampness makes stools loose and heavy, and leaves you feeling bloated and fatigued. If Dampness combines with Heat - often from rich, spicy foods or long-standing emotional heat - it settles in the Large Intestine, causing urgent, burning, foul-smelling diarrhea. On the other hand, if the body’s fluids are depleted (through Yin deficiency or excessive dryness), the Large Intestine loses its lubrication, leading to dry, pellet-like constipation.
Each of these patterns - and the deeper deficiency patterns involving Kidney Yang - represents a different root cause. That’s why two people with the same IBS diagnosis might need completely opposite treatments: one needs cooling and drying, another needs warming and moistening. TCM doesn’t just chase symptoms; it reads the body’s signals to restore the balance that keeps the gut calm.
classical_quote: 「The Liver is the general from whom planning emanates... The Spleen and Stomach are the granaries from which the five flavors are derived.」
classical_translation: "This passage establishes the Liver's command over the smooth flow of Qi and the Spleen's role in digestion. When the general (Liver) is overbearing, it attacks the granary (Spleen), a dynamic that underpins intestinal dysautonomia with alternating bowel habits and stress-triggered pain."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking about bowel habits, pain, and emotional triggers. If stress or frustration brings on cramping, alternating loose stools and constipation, and relief after a bowel movement, the pattern is Rebellious Liver Qi invading the Spleen (肝气乘脾, gān qì chéng pí). The tongue often looks pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse may feel wiry on the left and relaxed on the right.
When the main issue is persistent loose stools, a heavy sensation in the limbs, and fatigue after eating, the diagnosis leans toward Spleen Deficiency with Dampness (脾虚湿盛, pí xū shī shèng). Here the Spleen cannot transform fluids, so dampness builds up. The tongue appears pale, swollen, and coated with a greasy white fur, and the pulse is soft and slow.
Sudden, urgent diarrhea that is foul-smelling, possibly with mucus and a burning anus, points to Damp-Heat in the Large Intestine (大肠湿热, dà cháng shī rè). This often flares after a rich meal or an infection. The tongue is red with a thick, yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse feels rapid and slippery.
When constipation dominates and stools are dry, hard, and pellet-like, the pattern is Large Intestine Dryness (大肠燥热, dà cháng zào rè). This stems from fluid depletion or Yin deficiency. The tongue may be dry and red with little coating, and the pulse is thready.
Long-standing emotional tension can lead to Liver Qi Stagnation that transforms into Heat (肝郁化热, gān yù huà rè). Here constipation comes with irritability, a dry mouth, a bitter taste, and a bloated abdomen that feels warm or burning. The tongue is red with a yellow coating, and the pulse is wiry and rapid.
In chronic cases where the body’s warming energy is depleted, Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency (脾肾阳虚, pí shèn yáng xū) sets in. The hallmark is early-morning diarrhea, accompanied by cold limbs, a pale complexion, and deep exhaustion. The tongue is pale, swollen, and wet, and the pulse is deep and weak.

patterns.symptoms: ["Abdominal pain that leads to diarrhea", "Diarrhea triggered by emotional upset", "Pain relief after bowel movement", "Rib-side distension and fullness", "Alternating constipation and loose stools", "Irritability and frequent sighing"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, Anger or frustration, Cold or raw foods, Irregular eating, Overeating
patterns.better_with: Stress reduction, Warm, cooked meals, Light exercise like walking, Regular meal times
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver is responsible for keeping Qi moving smoothly. When stress or frustration builds up, Liver Qi stagnates and then surges sideways, attacking the Spleen. This disrupts the Spleen's ability to transform food and fluids, so the intestines react with cramping and urgent diarrhea-often right after an emotional upset. Once the bowel empties, the pressure eases and the pain fades, but the cycle returns whenever tension rises.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale body, possible teeth marks at the edges, thin white coating that may be slightly greasy. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) overall, distinctly wiry at the left middle (Liver) position, and softer at the right middle (Spleen) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress and anger directly surge Liver Qi, which then invades the Spleen and triggers intestinal cramping and diarrhea-the very mechanism of this pattern. Calming the mind and soothing the Liver removes the trigger. Warm, regular meals support the Spleen's digestive function, while cold and raw foods weaken it further, making the gut more reactive to emotional swings.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals at regular times; avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen. Gentle daily movement like walking helps keep Qi flowing. Build in small stress breaks-deep breathing or a short walk-especially before meals.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen’s Qi is too weak to transform and transport fluids, water and moisture build up inside the body as internal Dampness. This Dampness sits heavily in the digestive system, clogging the normal movement of Qi and making the intestines sluggish and waterlogged. The result is loose, unformed stools, a feeling of bloating that gets worse after eating, and a heavy, tired sensation in the body and limbs.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks and a white greasy coating that looks moist. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slow (Huan), may feel slippery; deep and weak if deficiency is pronounced.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dampness is a heavy, yin pathogen that thrives on cold and moisture. Warm, cooked foods and a dry environment help the Spleen function better and dry out excess Dampness. Overeating or eating hard-to-digest foods overwhelms the weak Spleen, creating more stagnation and loose stools. Gentle movement circulates Qi and helps shift fluid buildup, while rest allows the Spleen to recover its energy.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like soups, congee, and steamed vegetables. Avoid cold, raw, greasy, and dairy-heavy foods that create more Dampness. Gentle daily movement, such as walking or stretching, helps keep Qi and fluids moving. Try not to overeat and allow time for rest after meals.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Dampness and Heat combine in the body, they can settle in the Large Intestine and disrupt its normal function. This often happens after eating too many greasy, spicy, or rich foods, or when emotional stress generates Heat that mixes with internal Dampness. The Damp-Heat irritates the intestinal lining, causing urgent, foul-smelling diarrhea with mucus or blood, a burning sensation at the anus, and a feeling of incomplete evacuation. In intestinal dysautonomia, this pattern typically appears as acute flare-ups that alternate with periods of relative calm.

patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy, and rich foods create Dampness and Heat in the body, which then lodge in the Large Intestine, aggravating the symptoms. Cooling, bland foods and hydration help clear Heat and drain Dampness, while rest allows the body to recover and reduces internal friction.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat a light, bland diet with plenty of cooked vegetables and congee. Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and sugary foods, as well as alcohol and coffee. Drink plenty of warm water or barley tea to help flush out Damp-Heat. Gentle exercise like walking can help move Qi, but avoid overheating.

Stress and overwork further deplete Yin, while regular meals and gentle movement support the Spleen's ability to produce fluids.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink plenty of warm water and eat moistening foods such as pears, honey, and sesame. Avoid spicy, fried, and dry foods that deplete fluids. Gentle abdominal massage and regular light exercise can help stimulate bowel movements.

patterns.why_this_happens: When frustration and emotional stress are held in for too long, Liver Qi stagnates. Over time this stuck energy generates heat, like friction creating a spark. That heat dries up the fluids that normally keep the intestines moist and moving, leading to constipation with dry, hard stools. The heat also rises, causing irritability, a bitter taste, and a burning sensation in the abdomen.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, especially red at the sides, with a yellow coating. Pulse: wiry and rapid (弦数 xián shuò), forceful at the left middle position.

Spicy and greasy foods, alcohol, and emotional upset all add more heat and keep the Qi stuck, making the constipation and irritability worse. Cooling foods and stress reduction help clear the heat and allow the Qi to flow smoothly again, which naturally moistens the intestines and calms the mind.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat plenty of cooling, moistening foods like cucumber, celery, pear, and spinach. Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods that add heat. Cut back on alcohol and coffee. Practice daily stress management through meditation, gentle walking, or tai chi, and keep regular meal times to help the Liver and Spleen work in harmony.

patterns.symptoms: ["Diarrhea at dawn (around 5 AM)", "Cold hands and feet, especially below knees", "Sore and cold lower back and knees", "Undigested food in stools", "Abdominal cold pain that improves with warmth", "Frequent urination with clear, pale urine"]

patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yang is the body's root fire, responsible for warming all organs. When it weakens, it fails to warm the Spleen, causing Spleen Yang deficiency. The digestive fire cannot transform food and fluids, leading to chronic loose stools, undigested food, and cold pain in the abdomen. The Kidney's gate of life fire is weakest at dawn, so diarrhea often strikes early in the morning, leaving the intestines sluggish and cold.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and swollen with teeth marks on the sides and a white, slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak, and slow; both rear (Chi) positions are notably feeble, and the right middle (Guan) position feels soft and lacks root.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney and Spleen Yang deficiency means the body's warming fire is low. Cold and raw foods, cold weather, and overwork further extinguish that fire, worsening diarrhea and coldness. Warmth, rest, and warm foods help conserve and gently replenish Yang, allowing the digestive system to function.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat only warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees; avoid all raw, cold, and iced items. Keep the abdomen and lower back warm with a belly band or hot water bottle. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps circulation without depleting energy. Moxibustion on the lower abdomen and lower back can be very helpful.

faqs.question: How does acupuncture help IBS?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture helps regulate the nervous system, reduce visceral hypersensitivity, and restore the smooth flow of Qi through the digestive tract. Points like Zusanli (ST-36) and Tianshu (ST-25) directly calm the intestines and strengthen the Spleen, while Taichong (LR-3) eases Liver Qi stagnation - the root of stress-triggered symptoms. Most patients feel deeply relaxed during treatment, and many notice their gut “settle” after just a few sessions.

faqs.question: Can TCM treat constipation-predominant IBS?
faqs.answer: Yes. TCM treats constipation not with a single laxative but by identifying why the bowel is dry or sluggish. If it’s due to Liver Qi stagnation generating Heat, we clear the Heat and move the Qi. If it’s from fluid deficiency (Large Intestine Dryness), we nourish Yin and moisten the intestines. Acupuncture points like Zhigou (SJ-6) and Sanyinjiao (SP-6) are especially effective for promoting bowel movements without causing dependency.

faqs.question: What herbs are commonly used for IBS with diarrhea?
faqs.answer: The classic formula is Tong Xie Yao Fang (Pain and Diarrhea Formula), which contains Bai Shao (white peony root) to soothe the Liver, Bai Zhu (Atractylodes) to strengthen the Spleen, Chen Pi (tangerine peel) to regulate Qi, and Fang Feng (Saposhnikovia) to harmonize the Liver and Spleen. It’s specifically designed for stress-related cramping and loose stools. For Damp-Heat diarrhea, Ge Gen Qin Lian Tang is used to clear Heat and dry Dampness.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet completely?
faqs.answer: You don’t need a drastic overhaul, but some adjustments help the herbs work better. Generally, we recommend eating warm, cooked meals and avoiding raw, cold, and greasy foods - these tax the Spleen. As your digestion strengthens, you’ll likely be able to tolerate a wider variety of foods again. The goal is to restore your digestive resilience, not to keep you on a restrictive diet forever.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with TCM?
faqs.answer: Many people notice less bloating and pain within 2-4 weeks, with bowel movements becoming more regular. For stress-triggered patterns, improvement can be quite rapid once the Liver is soothed. Deeper deficiency patterns, like Kidney Yang Deficiency with early-morning diarrhea, take longer - often 3-6 months of consistent treatment to rebuild the body’s core warmth. Your practitioner will track your tongue and pulse to monitor progress even before symptoms fully resolve.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe to use alongside my IBS medications?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. Herbs and acupuncture can complement antispasmodics, fiber supplements, and low-dose antidepressants. However, always tell both your TCM practitioner and your medical doctor about everything you’re taking. If you’re on strong prescription medications for diarrhea or constipation, your TCM practitioner will likely adjust the herbal formula to avoid over-treatment and may suggest a gradual reduction of pharmaceuticals as your gut function stabilizes - but only under your doctor’s guidance.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with the anxiety that triggers my IBS?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM doesn’t separate the mind and body - the Liver is the organ most affected by stress, and when its Qi stagnates, it directly impacts the intestines. Acupuncture points like Yintang (between the eyebrows) and Shenmen (HT-7) calm the spirit, while herbs in formulas like Xiao Yao San smooth the Liver and relieve emotional tension. As your Liver Qi flows more freely, you may find that stressful situations no longer send you running to the bathroom.

research.title: Tong Xie Yao Fang: A Classic Chinese Medicine Prescription with Potential for the Treatment of Ulcerative Colitis
research.description: This review article examines the pharmacological mechanisms of Tong Xie Yao Fang in modulating intestinal inflammation, visceral hypersensitivity, and gut motility. It highlights the formula's ability to regulate the brain-gut axis, making it relevant for stress-related intestinal dysautonomia and diarrhea-predominant IBS.
research.periodical: Li X, et al. Tong Xie Yao Fang: A Classic Chinese Medicine Prescription with Potential for the Treatment of Ulcerative Colitis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2021.

research.title: Acupuncture for irritable bowel syndrome: systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A Cochrane systematic review that pooled data from multiple RCTs. It found that acupuncture significantly improved IBS symptoms and quality of life compared to sham acupuncture or conventional medication, with a favorable safety profile. The review supports acupuncture as a viable option for functional bowel disorders that correspond to TCM patterns like Liver invading Spleen.
research.periodical: Manheimer E, et al. Acupuncture for irritable bowel syndrome. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012.

research.title: 针灸治疗肝郁脾虚型肠易激综合征疗效及机制探讨 (Efficacy and mechanism of acupuncture for IBS of Liver-depression and Spleen-deficiency type)
research.description: A clinical trial investigating the effects of acupuncture on IBS patients with the Liver-depression and Spleen-deficiency pattern. Results showed significant improvement in abdominal pain, bowel frequency, and emotional symptoms, with mechanisms linked to regulation of serotonin and brain-gut peptides.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. 针灸治疗肝郁脾虚型肠易激综合征疗效及机制探讨. Chinese Acupuncture & Moxibustion. 2019.
